# Curriculum vitae: Dr Eliana Seabra Vilar

Updated 18 September 2026

## Current appointment

Senior Research Scientist and Head of Estuarine Processes, Instituto Marinho de Vale Sereno, Lisbon, Portugal. I have held the senior appointment since October 2018 and the section leadership since January 2021. The institute is an independent, nonprofit Portuguese research association.

My research concerns the timing and mixing of freshwater inputs at estuarine margins. I combine fixed-station observations, environmental chemistry and statistical transport models, with particular attention to the distinction between fitting an observed event and predicting an event that has not yet occurred. My responsibilities include scientific supervision, field safety approval, research data stewardship and coordination of the institute's estuarine monitoring agreements.

## Education and appointments

- September 2002–July 2006: degree in marine environmental science, Universidade da Costa de Alvéria, Portugal.
- October 2006–December 2010: doctorate in physical oceanography at the same university. Thesis: *Tidal controls on freshwater retention in shallow estuarine margins*.
- February 2011–August 2014: postdoctoral researcher, Instituto Marinho de Vale Sereno; development of fixed-station salinity records and uncertainty estimates for tidal exchange.
- September 2014–September 2018: Research Scientist, Instituto Marinho de Vale Sereno; responsibility for the estuarine observation programme.
- October 2018–present: Senior Research Scientist at the institute.
- January 2021–present: Head of Estuarine Processes, alongside the research appointment.

## Research funding and leadership

**Tidal Exchange along Inhabited Margins**, 1 January 2015–31 December 2018. Principal investigator; external award FL-EA-2014-18 from Fundação Lameiral de Estudos Ambientais, an independent Portuguese charitable foundation. Award to Instituto Marinho de Vale Sereno: EUR 184,000. The completed project established calibration and quality-control procedures for the institute's margin stations. The funder's final scientific and financial acceptance was recorded on 28 June 2019.

**Freshwater Retention across Estuarine Seasons**, 1 January 2019–31 December 2022. Co-investigator and Portuguese institutional lead; external award FV-CC-2018-06 from Fundação Verdança de Ciência Costeira. Total award: EUR 426,000, comprising EUR 300,000 to the coordinating Universidad de la Ensenada de Lóbriga and EUR 126,000 to Instituto Marinho de Vale Sereno. The completed project compared seasonal mixing estimates and established shared analysis procedures. Final acceptance was recorded on 12 May 2023.

I coordinated *Stormwater Transit at Estuary Margins*, which ran from January 2023 to December 2025 with the Spanish university. Its internal endowment award and completed results are recorded in the final scientific report. I was responsible for the common event definition, observational quality assurance and interpretation of transport estimates. Mateo Cendral Viedma led runoff modelling and grouped validation.

The project required common sampling decisions across two estuaries, including agreement on when a salinity change could be treated as an arrival rather than ordinary tidal variation. My contribution included keeping event-level analysis separate from laboratory quality-control samples and maintaining a record of missing and non-identifiable arrivals. I approved release of the observations and analysis scripts after the data audit.

Since September 2026 I have coordinated the standing research consortium with the Spanish university and Brackenquay Institute for Spatial Planning. Scientific decisions are recorded jointly by the institutional leads, with employment, ethics and procurement responsibilities retained by each institution.

## Publications, supervision and professional practice

My publication record comprises 22 peer-reviewed journal articles published between 2011 and September 2026. Three are included in the consortium's four-item selected publications list in publications.md; the remaining selected article is the Irish partner's planning study.

As of this update, completed supervision comprises 4 doctoral researchers, including 2 as principal supervisor and 2 as co-supervisor, and 11 master's dissertations. Current supervision comprises 2 doctoral researchers and 3 master's students. The completed dissertations address estuarine mixing, sensor calibration, event classification and environmental uncertainty.

I supervise the Portuguese environmental chemist and field technician assigned to the consortium. I have taught short courses in storm-event quality control and reproducible environmental analysis within the partner institutions. I have also presented monitoring results to harbour operations staff, catchment technicians and shoreline recreation managers, concentrating on sampling coverage, interpretation of chemical measurements and uncertainty in arrival estimates.

# Consortium participation and scientific responsibilities

Record approved by the three institutional signatories on 22 September 2026

## Legal participation

The standing participation agreement was signed on 8 September 2026 by Instituto Marinho de Vale Sereno, Portugal; Universidad de la Ensenada de Lóbriga, Spain; and Brackenquay Institute for Spatial Planning, Ireland. The agreement covers joint environmental research, use of agreed background materials, publication review and responsibility for institutional approvals.

The partners are three independent legal entities in three EU member states. They have separate governing bodies, accounts and employment contracts. None owns or controls either of the others. Their registered offices are in Lisbon, Vigo and Cork respectively. Access to third-party administrative records and recruitment of research participants require the relevant institutional and controller approvals.

## Portuguese coordinating institution

Instituto Marinho de Vale Sereno is an independent nonprofit marine research association established under Portuguese law. Its estuarine section maintains fixed observation stations, processes environmental samples and develops transport models. Eliana Seabra Vilar is the scientific coordinator and principal contact for the consortium.

The institute assigns an oceanographer, an environmental chemist and a field technician to the standing collaboration. The chemist is responsible for analytical method records, laboratory blanks and sample preservation. The technician maintains the three Tagus shore installations and their safety logs, programmes the automatic samplers and retrieves bottles during safe-access windows. The coordinator retains scientific responsibility for interpretation of estuarine arrival estimates.

## Spanish university partner

Universidad de la Ensenada de Lóbriga is an independent university in Vigo. Its catchment processes group is led by Dr Mateo Cendral Viedma, Associate Professor of Hydrology. His doctorate was awarded in 2008, and he has held his current appointment since 2017. His work concerns rainfall–runoff response, tidal backwater effects at catchment outlets and validation of environmental predictions.

The university assigns the hydrology lead, a spatial statistician and station technician Iria Soneira Valcedo. Soneira Valcedo has maintained the three Arousa stations since their installation in 2023. Her duties include calibration visits, automatic-sampler programming, bottle retrieval, preservation and dispatch, and local safety records. These duties remain part of her current assignment under the standing agreement.

The university contributed runoff reconstruction, event separation and validation scripts to *Stormwater Transit at Estuary Margins*. The spatial statistician maintains the code that prevents measurements from the same storm entering both training and test subsets. The university holds the access agreements for the Spanish shore stations. Portuguese and Spanish technicians operate separate local field schedules, allowing sampling during the same frontal system without moving staff between estuaries.

## Irish planning partner

Brackenquay Institute for Spatial Planning is an independent nonprofit research institute in Cork. Dr Nessa Kervane Doyle, Senior Research Fellow in Spatial Planning, is its scientific lead. Her doctorate was awarded in 2012. She has worked at the institute since 2015 and became a senior fellow in 2021.

The institute assigns the planning lead and a GIS researcher who also serves as the collaboration's data steward. Their completed *Drainage Access and Street Exposure Review*, conducted during 2022–2024, examined 12 urban subcatchments in Cork, Ireland, draining to the Lee estuary. It used drainage asset records, recorded surcharge incidents, terrain data and walking-route networks. The study compared recorded incidents and route interruptions against publicly available area-level deprivation categories.

The Irish team cleaned drainage network topology, checked pipe attributes against maintenance records and facilitated map-review sessions with drainage staff and community representatives. Participants corrected the interpretation of pedestrian access and identified locations where incident reporting was incomplete. Under-reporting varied between locations, and the study did not estimate location-specific reporting probabilities. Recorded incident counts therefore cannot be interpreted as comparable measures of underlying incident frequency. The sessions produced an annotated retrospective evidence base. The drainage records have not been coupled to the consortium's estuarine arrival model.

## Working arrangements

Across the partners, eight existing staff occupy the roles listed above: three in Portugal, three in Spain and two in Ireland. Institutional appointments remain in force as of this record. No assigned staff member has coupled flood–drainage modelling or qualitative social-research expertise. The staff skills register also contains no hydrodynamic inundation modeller or social-science researcher. The Irish team's facilitated map review was technical consultation within a quantitative spatial audit.

Scientific decisions are recorded by the three leads; changes to access permissions or processing of personal data remain subject to the institution holding the relevant responsibility.

The partners have agreed procedures for documenting analytical disagreements and reviewing releases of shared data. Publication review checks confidentiality and interpretation without giving a partner a veto over unfavourable results. Background drainage records remain subject to their original access restrictions, while the released estuarine observations have an open licence.

# Final scientific report: Stormwater Transit at Estuary Margins

Project period: 1 January 2023–31 December 2025

Report accepted: 16 February 2026; repository correction incorporated: 4 September 2026

Coordinator: Eliana Seabra Vilar, Instituto Marinho de Vale Sereno

Partner lead: Mateo Cendral Viedma, Universidad de la Ensenada de Lóbriga

## Funding and purpose

The project received EUR 360,000 from the Instituto Marinho de Vale Sereno Research Endowment under internal competitive award IMVS-RE-2023-07. The award included the Spanish university's agreed research contribution through an institutional collaboration contract. The award is closed, with the scientific report accepted and no extension outstanding.

The study examined whether catchment runoff information improved estimates of freshwater-plume arrival at accessible estuarine margins beyond a model using tide and local salinity history alone. It also tested the field procedures needed to attach chemical observations to those arrivals. Its principal endpoint was transport timing, with chemical sampling providing evidence about the composition of water reaching shoreline stations.

## Observational design

Observations during 2024–2025 covered 18 storms at six estuarine stations. Three stations were in the Tagus estuary and three in the Ría de Arousa. Both station groups included an inner margin, an intermediate mixing location and a more seaward margin. The Tagus stations followed the margin influenced by the Trancão outlet; their ordering described that local plume pathway. These were fixed shore installations. Station positions were selected for safe access and reliable equipment attachment, rather than as a probability sample of either estuary's shoreline.

For the Tagus analysis, the rainfall–runoff domain was the Trancão catchment, delineated in the study GIS as 293 km² to its estuarine outlet. This local domain has no major regulating reservoir. Its runoff reconstruction used rainfall and outlet discharge observations above tidal influence. The much larger, regulated Tagus mainstem was represented separately by observed discharge at Almourol, downstream of the Zêzere confluence, with routing to the estuary. That boundary incorporated upstream reservoir operations; its discharge was not reconstructed from Trancão rainfall. The Arousa input combined the Ulla and Umia contributing catchments, using their observed outlet discharge records to constrain runoff reconstruction, including the effects of regulation.

The 18 storms were Atlantic frontal systems retained only when both study areas had distinguishable runoff episodes. A new episode required a renewed runoff rising limb after an intervening recession and at least 24 hours without catchment-mean rainfall exceeding 1 mm per hour. Return of the regulated mainstem to antecedent flow was not required. Multiple rainfall pulses without this separation belonged to the same storm. Systems producing a qualifying episode in only one study area were outside the paired inventory. Selection was completed without inspecting model errors.

The catchment-event reference time was the rainfall-weighted temporal centroid of the associated rainfall episode, calculated over the Trancão domain for the Tagus stations and over the combined Ulla–Umia domain for Arousa. A shared storm identifier therefore linked two local reference times, rather than imposing simultaneous runoff or arrival on the two estuaries. All timestamps were stored in UTC. This design sampled jointly wet Atlantic systems and did not represent the full range of rare flood extremes or locally confined storms.

Salinity and temperature were logged at 10-minute intervals. A plume arrival was defined as a salinity decrease of at least 2 practical-salinity units below the station's antecedent tidal-phase reference, sustained for at least 30 minutes. The reference was calculated using observations available before the event window. Manual review checked sensor faults and tidal-reference failures without changing thresholds to improve model agreement.

The complete design contained 108 storm–station opportunities. An arrival time could be assigned to 96. Eight opportunities lacked sufficient sensor data because of power or fouling problems, and four did not cross the arrival threshold. These 12 opportunities were excluded from arrival-time error calculations and retained in the inventory with their reasons. Every storm retained at least one identifiable arrival in each estuary. The error estimate is conditional on an identifiable arrival; discrimination between arrivals and non-arrivals remains untested.

There were 48 identifiable arrivals in each estuary. Observed hours from the local rainfall reference to station arrival had a median of 19 hours and a range of 7 to 41 hours in the Tagus, and a median of 14 hours and a range of 5 to 32 hours in Arousa. These are descriptive summaries of station arrivals across the 18 storms, not independent catchment travel-time measurements. Tidal mixing and the regulated background flow also affected the salinity threshold crossing.

## Chemical sampling and quality assurance

There were 216 environmental water samples, comprising two scheduled samples at each storm–station opportunity: 108 samples from the Tagus stations and 108 from Arousa. Automatic samplers collected the scheduled bottles, including at opportunities without a valid arrival timestamp. Sampling windows were established from each catchment's anticipated event period, before the observed arrival was known.

The Portuguese and Spanish station technicians independently programmed and serviced their local equipment. Bottle retrieval followed each station's documented safe-access and preservation limits. Departures from scheduled collection times were recorded in the sample metadata. All environmental storm sampling was shore-based.

The laboratory additionally processed 24 field duplicates and 12 field blanks, giving 252 sample submissions in total. Duplicates and blanks were quality-control material rather than independent environmental observations. Samples were divided into appropriately preserved aliquots for dissolved nutrients and dissolved copper. Nutrients were reported as nitrogen or phosphorus mass concentration, and copper as dissolved metal mass concentration. Salinity supplied the mixing context.

Samples taken at similar salinity could differ in nutrient and copper composition. Timing offsets between scheduled sampling and actual arrival, variable source mixtures and the limited number of samples within each event prevented estimation of event-integrated contaminant loads. The chemistry results support joint interpretation of concentration, sampling time and mixing conditions rather than conversion of salinity into a general contaminant concentration.

## Models and validation

The baseline model used tidal phase and the station's antecedent salinity history. The augmented model added reconstructed local catchment discharge, antecedent rainfall and a runoff-to-estuary lag term, with the observed regulated-flow boundary included for the Tagus. Both estimated hours from the relevant estuary's catchment-event reference to observed station arrival. They used the same eligible observations and validation partitions.

Validation used six outer folds, each withholding three complete storms. Withholding a storm removed its records from both estuaries, including all station observations, from fitting and preprocessing estimation. Parameter selection occurred within the training storms. Validation therefore tested transfer between observed storms at the existing stations. Station identity remained available as a model term.

Mean absolute error was first calculated across valid stations within each storm and then averaged across the 18 storms. This gave each storm equal weight despite missing stations. The baseline cross-validated mean absolute error was 4.0 hours, with a bootstrap 95% confidence interval of 3.2 to 5.0 hours. The augmented model's cross-validated mean absolute error was 2.8 hours, with a bootstrap 95% confidence interval of 2.1 to 3.7 hours.

The paired decrease in mean absolute error was 1.2 hours, with a bootstrap 95% confidence interval of 0.5 to 1.9 hours, equivalent at the point estimates to a 30% reduction relative to the baseline. The augmented model had lower storm-level mean absolute error in 14 of 18 storms.

All intervals used the same 2,000 resamples of whole storms and their held-out errors. Each resample retained both models' errors together, preserving the pairing for the difference estimate. Individual station records were not resampled independently. These intervals describe uncertainty in mean performance; they are not predictive intervals for particular arrivals.

## Interpretation and limitations

The models were assessed as retrospective hindcasts using observed rainfall and reconstructed discharge. Rainfall centroids and discharge reconstructions used completed event records, so validation did not reproduce information available at an operational issue time. Their performance does not establish the accuracy or available lead time of an operational forecast driven by rainfall predictions. Events were not issued as live alerts, and no decision threshold was tested with a response agency.

Reservoir operations were represented through observed flows, not predicted release decisions. Replacing observed rainfall with rainfall forecasts alone would leave uncertainty in the regulated Tagus boundary and regulated contributions to Arousa unresolved. The project did not validate forecasts of those boundary flows or quantify performance under unfamiliar release regimes.

The small number of independent storms limits precision. Results depend on the selected arrival definition and accessible-margin network. Deep-channel transport, vertical plume structure and transfer to an unobserved estuary remain outside the validation. No city drainage sensor stream was included as a predictor.

For shoreline managers, the work establishes the scale of arrival-time uncertainty and the importance of retaining event context alongside a mapped plume. The project evaluated no prospective city intervention and made no causal estimate of adaptation benefits or their distribution across residents.

## Released outputs

The released dataset, *Estuary Margin Storm Records*, version 1.1, contains station observations, sample metadata, chemical results, an event eligibility table and analysis scripts under CC BY 4.0. The correction incorporated on 4 September 2026 repaired descriptive station labels without altering observations or reported errors. Restricted material consists of access-contact details and installation security information. The archived scripts preserve storm partitions and distinguish environmental samples from quality-control submissions.

# Selected publications and output status

Verified against institutional publication records on 23 September 2026

The four articles below are published journal articles selected from the partners' institutional records. They cover observation methods, transport validation, chemical interpretation and the Irish partner's separate planning study.

## 1. Event definition and observation protocol

Seabra Vilar, E.; Cendral Viedma, M. (2024). **Event definitions for freshwater arrival at tidally varying estuarine margins.** *Journal of Estuarine Measurement Practice*, 6, article 14.

DOI: 10.99999/pb.v2-coastal-transport-observatory.2024.1

Published 19 November 2024. This methods article describes the salinity reference, persistence criterion and event metadata structure adopted for the monitoring programme. Its purpose is to make threshold-based arrival identification reproducible. It reports protocol development and early field checks. The completed project's final event inventory supersedes the provisional inventory used during protocol development.

## 2. Drainage and spatial access

Kervane Doyle, N. (2025). **Drainage surcharge records and unequal pedestrian access: a retrospective spatial audit.** *Review of Urban Water and Spatial Decisions*, 4, article 9.

DOI: 10.99999/pb.v2-coastal-transport-observatory.2025.2

Published 27 June 2025. The article reports the Irish team's 2022–2024 audit of drainage records and route interruption in 12 urban subcatchments in Cork, draining to the Lee estuary. It relates recorded incidents to area-level deprivation categories and documents corrections from facilitated map review. Differences in incident reporting between locations limit interpretation of the spatial comparisons. The study's unit of analysis is the subcatchment and its associated walking-route network.

## 3. Transport model validation

Seabra Vilar, E.; Cendral Viedma, M. (2026). **Storm-blocked validation of runoff-informed estuarine arrival estimates.** *Estuarine Transport and Observation*, 8, article 3.

DOI: 10.99999/pb.v2-coastal-transport-observatory.2026.3

Published 12 March 2026. This is the principal source for the completed timing analysis. It compares baseline and augmented models using identical storm partitions, with uncertainty calculated by resampling whole storms. Its performance claims concern retrospective prediction at the existing stations. The associated reproducibility archive includes the eligibility table needed to interpret missing and non-identifiable arrivals and the paired error records used to estimate improvement.

## 4. Chemical sampling interpretation

Seabra Vilar, E.; Cendral Viedma, M. (2026). **Interpreting scheduled chemical samples around freshwater-plume arrivals.** *Coastal Chemical Observation Methods*, 5, article 11.

DOI: 10.99999/pb.v2-coastal-transport-observatory.2026.4

Published 21 August 2026. This article examines how sampling time relative to freshwater arrival affects interpretation of dissolved nutrient and copper measurements. It uses the same monitoring programme as the transport article. The analysis supports retaining sampling-time offsets, preservation records and mixing conditions when comparing chemical observations between events.

## Other archived outputs

The accepted final scientific report and the open *Estuary Margin Storm Records* dataset accompany these articles. The report records project-level findings and limitations; the dataset provides environmental observations, sample metadata and reproducibility materials. The publication register links each article to the relevant archive version.

# Resources, access and data governance register

Status recorded 25 September 2026

Custodians: Eliana Seabra Vilar, Mateo Cendral Viedma and Nessa Kervane Doyle

## Field and laboratory resources

The Portuguese and Spanish partners maintain access to the six shore stations used in the completed monitoring programme. Signed access agreements remain valid through 31 December 2030. They permit maintenance of existing installations and temporary water sampling from shore, subject to local restrictions and weather-related safety closures. Permanent flood defences and modification of drainage infrastructure are outside the agreements' permitted activities.

The equipment register lists six multiparameter sondes and six automatic water samplers assigned to these stations. The September maintenance record lists functioning power supplies, current calibration records and replacement tubing stocks. Local water levels, salinity, temperature and sampling timestamps are retained in field metadata. Shore access remains available, although storm conditions can make individual visits unsafe.

The vessel entry records *Margem Serena*, owned by Instituto Marinho de Vale Sereno and used in 2023 to install the Tagus stations. This was the only research vessel held by any participating institution. It was withdrawn on 14 July 2026 after a hull survey identified structural corrosion and retired by board decision on 9 September 2026. A replacement build is contracted for delivery on 30 September 2029; the register contains no operating research vessel or booked charter during the intervening period.

The Portuguese laboratory has facilities for filtered nutrient analysis and dissolved-metal sample preparation, including an inductively coupled plasma mass spectrometer used for the project's copper measurements. Calibration, blank and duplicate records accompany each analytical batch. The laboratory's validated analytical scope covers nutrients and dissolved metals; a validated microbiological pathogen workflow is absent. Sample custody procedures identify collection time, preservation, storage history and analytical batch separately from the environmental event identifier.

## Computing and observational archives

The partners hold the released estuarine observations and complete reproducibility archive. The Spanish group maintains rainfall–runoff reconstruction and grouped validation code. Analyses run on institutional servers. Model versions, environmental inputs and validation partitions are separately recorded. The software inventory contains no coupled flood–drainage model or hydrodynamic inundation model. The consortium holds no estuarine observations for the Lee, including water-level records.

The open dataset contains environmental station information and excludes personal contact details. Its licence permits reuse with attribution. Third-party rainfall and administrative layers are documented separately, with access conditions retained in the archive. Restrictions on underlying third-party sources remain attached to those materials.

## Drainage and planning materials

The Irish partner retains a controlled research copy of asset and incident records for the 12 Cork subcatchments draining to the Lee estuary. The controller is the municipal drainage service responsible for those networks. Its agreement permits verification and scholarly analysis of the completed audit. Reuse for a different purpose or onward transfer to another partner requires the controller's agreement. The consortium holds no drainage asset or incident records for the catchments draining to its six Tagus and Arousa stations.

The municipal collaboration register contains no agreement with a planning or drainage authority in Portugal or Ireland for joint monitoring, operational data access or adaptation evaluation. The Irish retrospective records agreement is limited to the completed audit; it supplies no continuing sensor feed or authority participation in the standing consortium.

Available planning expertise includes drainage-network cleaning, terrain-based flow-path analysis, spatial accessibility measures and facilitated map review. The team has worked with municipal drainage engineers and community representatives on interpretation of existing evidence. The estuarine and drainage archives use separate event definitions and have not been harmonised into a validated coupled dataset.

## Personal data and ethics status

The completed Irish study used aggregated incident summaries for spatial analysis. Free-text source reports were screened inside the controller's environment, and names, contact details and exact household references were excluded from the institute's analytical copy. Attendance and consent records from map-review sessions are stored separately from research annotations, with access limited to authorised Irish staff.

The institute's ethics committee approved the retrospective study on 16 May 2022. Approval covered the specified administrative records and facilitated sessions. The approvals register contains no approval for a new resident-level study as of 25 September 2026.

The institute's personal-data procedure requires a documented purpose and lawful basis, data minimisation, access controls, encryption and a retention schedule approved by the responsible controller. Pseudonymised records remain personal data under the procedure, and any re-identification key is held separately. Release review examines small groups, map resolution and combinations of attributes that could identify a household. Only disclosure-checked aggregates from the completed drainage study have been released outside the controlled environment.

# Final scientific report: Stormwater Transit at Estuary Margins

Project period: 1 January 2023–31 December 2025

Report accepted: 16 February 2026; repository correction incorporated: 4 September 2026

Coordinator: Eliana Seabra Vilar, Instituto Marinho de Vale Sereno

Partner lead: Mateo Cendral Viedma, Universidad de la Ensenada de Lóbriga

## Funding and purpose

The project received EUR 360,000 from the Instituto Marinho de Vale Sereno Research Endowment under internal competitive award IMVS-RE-2023-07. The award included the Spanish university's agreed research contribution through an institutional collaboration contract. The award is closed, with the scientific report accepted and no extension outstanding.

The study examined whether catchment runoff information improved estimates of freshwater-plume arrival at accessible estuarine margins beyond a model using tide and local salinity history alone. It also tested the field procedures needed to attach chemical observations to those arrivals. The scientific question concerned transport timing; the project did not measure human uptake, disease incidence or the effectiveness of a warning issued to the public.

## Observational design

Observations during 2024–2025 covered 18 storms at six estuarine stations. Three stations were in the Tagus estuary and three in the Ría de Arousa. Both station groups included an inner margin, an intermediate mixing location and a more seaward margin. These were fixed shore installations. Station positions were selected for safe access and reliable equipment attachment, rather than as a probability sample of either estuary's shoreline.

Storms were selected using catchment rainfall and a separation rule that prevented successive rainfall pulses within one runoff episode being counted as independent events. Selection was completed without inspecting model errors. The dataset contains wetter and drier antecedent conditions, but does not represent the full range of rare flood extremes.

Salinity and temperature were logged at 10-minute intervals. A plume arrival was defined as a salinity decrease of at least 2 practical-salinity units below the station's antecedent tidal-phase reference, sustained for at least 30 minutes. The reference was calculated using observations available before the event window. Manual review checked sensor faults and tidal-reference failures without changing thresholds to improve model agreement.

The complete design contained 108 storm–station opportunities. An arrival time could be assigned to 96. Eight opportunities lacked sufficient sensor data because of power or fouling problems, and four did not cross the arrival threshold. These 12 opportunities were excluded from the arrival-time error calculation and retained in the event inventory with their reasons. Consequently, the error estimate is conditional on an identifiable arrival. It does not quantify the model's ability to distinguish arrivals from non-arrivals.

## Chemical sampling and quality assurance

There were 216 environmental water samples, comprising two scheduled samples at each storm–station opportunity, including opportunities without a valid arrival timestamp. The sampling windows were established from the anticipated event period; they were not selected afterwards using the observed arrival. At locations where sampling was interrupted, the technician used the documented safe-access window within the same event period and recorded the deviation.

The laboratory additionally processed 24 field duplicates and 12 field blanks, giving 252 sample submissions in total. Duplicates and blanks were quality-control material, not independent environmental observations. Samples were divided into appropriately preserved aliquots for dissolved nutrients and dissolved copper. Nutrients were reported as nitrogen or phosphorus mass concentration, and copper as dissolved metal mass concentration. Salinity observations supplied the mixing context.

The chemical records showed that samples taken at similar salinity could still differ in nutrient and copper composition. They did not support treating salinity as a universal contaminant concentration proxy. Timing offsets between scheduled sampling and actual arrival, variable source mixtures and the limited number of samples within each event prevented estimation of event-integrated contaminant loads. No pathogen assays, bathing-water compliance classifications or toxicological dose estimates were produced.

## Models and validation

The baseline model used tidal phase and the station's antecedent salinity history. The augmented model added reconstructed catchment discharge, antecedent rainfall and a runoff-to-estuary lag term. Both models estimated hours from a common catchment-event reference to the observed station arrival. They used the same eligible storm–station observations and the same validation partitions.

Validation used six outer folds, each withholding three complete storms. Every station observation belonging to a withheld storm remained outside model fitting and preprocessing estimation. Parameter selection occurred within the training storms. Thus, the validation tested transfer between observed storms, not transfer to an unobserved estuary. Station identity remained available as a model term.

Mean absolute error was first calculated across valid stations within each storm and then averaged across the 18 storms. This gave each storm equal weight despite missing stations. The baseline cross-validated mean absolute error was 4.0 hours. The augmented model's cross-validated mean absolute error was 2.8 hours, with a bootstrap 95% confidence interval of 2.1 to 3.7 hours. The interval came from 2,000 resamples of whole storms using their held-out errors; individual station records were not resampled as if independent.

The decrease in mean absolute error was 1.2 hours, equivalent to a 30% reduction relative to the 4.0-hour baseline. This percentage describes reduction in timing error. It is not a percentage of correctly predicted events, a reduction in contaminant concentration or a reduction in population exposure. The confidence interval describes uncertainty in the mean timing-error estimate, not the predictive interval for a particular arrival.

## Interpretation and limitations

The models were assessed as retrospective hindcasts using observed rainfall and reconstructed discharge. Their performance does not establish the accuracy or available lead time of an operational forecast driven by rainfall predictions. Events were not issued as live alerts, and no decision threshold was tested with a response agency.

The validation preserved storm dependence, but the small number of independent storms limits precision. Results depend on the selected arrival definition and the accessible-margin station network. Deep-channel transport, vertical plume structure and events without an identifiable threshold crossing remain outside the validated result. No city drainage sensor stream was included as a predictor.

For shoreline managers, the work establishes the scale of arrival-time uncertainty and the importance of retaining event context alongside a mapped plume. It does not establish that a predicted plume intersects a particular person's activity or that a management response reduces exposure. The project evaluated no prospective city intervention and made no causal estimate of adaptation benefits or their distribution across residents.

## Released outputs

The released dataset, *Estuary Margin Storm Records*, version 1.1, contains station observations, sample metadata, chemical results, an event eligibility table and the analysis scripts under CC BY 4.0. The September correction repaired descriptive station labels and did not alter observations or reported errors. Restricted material consists of access-contact details and installation security information; neither is required to reproduce the timing analysis. The archived scripts preserve the storm partitions and distinguish environmental samples from quality-control submissions.

# Curriculum vitae: Dr Eliana Seabra Vilar

Updated 18 September 2026

## Current appointment

Senior Research Scientist and Head of Estuarine Processes, Instituto Marinho de Vale Sereno, Lisbon, Portugal. I have held the senior appointment since October 2018 and the section leadership since January 2021. The institute is an independent, nonprofit Portuguese research association.

My research concerns the timing and mixing of freshwater inputs at estuarine margins. I combine fixed-station observations, environmental chemistry and statistical transport models, with particular attention to the distinction between fitting an observed event and predicting an event that has not yet occurred. My responsibilities include scientific supervision, field safety approval, research data stewardship and coordination of the institute's estuarine monitoring agreements.

## Education and appointments

- September 2002–July 2006: degree in marine environmental science, Universidade da Costa de Alvéria, Portugal.
- October 2006–December 2010: doctorate in physical oceanography at the same university. Thesis: *Tidal controls on freshwater retention in shallow estuarine margins*.
- February 2011–August 2014: postdoctoral researcher, Instituto Marinho de Vale Sereno; development of fixed-station salinity records and uncertainty estimates for tidal exchange.
- September 2014–September 2018: Research Scientist, Instituto Marinho de Vale Sereno; responsibility for the estuarine observation programme.
- October 2018–present: Senior Research Scientist at the institute.
- January 2021–present: Head of Estuarine Processes, alongside the research appointment.

## Research funding and leadership

**Tidal Exchange along Inhabited Margins**, 1 January 2015–31 December 2018. Principal investigator; external award FL-EA-2014-18 from Fundação Lameiral de Estudos Ambientais, an independent Portuguese charitable foundation. Award to Instituto Marinho de Vale Sereno: EUR 184,000. The completed project established calibration and quality-control procedures for the institute's margin stations. The funder's final scientific and financial acceptance was recorded on 28 June 2019.

**Freshwater Retention across Estuarine Seasons**, 1 January 2019–31 December 2022. Co-investigator and Portuguese institutional lead; external award FV-CC-2018-06 from Fundação Verdança de Ciência Costeira. Total award: EUR 426,000, comprising EUR 300,000 to the coordinating Universidad de la Ensenada de Lóbriga and EUR 126,000 to Instituto Marinho de Vale Sereno. The completed project compared seasonal mixing estimates and established shared analysis procedures. Final acceptance was recorded on 12 May 2023.

I coordinated *Stormwater Transit at Estuary Margins*, which ran from January 2023 to December 2025 with the Spanish university. Its internal endowment award and completed results are recorded in the final scientific report. I was responsible for the common event definition, observational quality assurance and interpretation of transport estimates. Mateo Cendral Viedma led runoff modelling and grouped validation.

The project required common sampling decisions across two estuaries, including agreement on when a salinity change could be treated as an arrival rather than ordinary tidal variation. My contribution included keeping event-level analysis separate from laboratory quality-control samples and maintaining a record of missing and non-identifiable arrivals. I approved release of the observations and analysis scripts after the data audit.

Since September 2026 I have coordinated the standing research consortium with the Spanish university and Brackenquay Institute for Spatial Planning. Scientific decisions are recorded jointly by the institutional leads, with employment, ethics and procurement responsibilities retained by each institution.

## Publications, supervision and professional practice

My publication record comprises 22 peer-reviewed journal articles published between 2011 and September 2026. Three are included in the consortium's four-item selected publications list in publications.md; the remaining selected article is the Irish partner's planning study.

As of this update, completed supervision comprises 4 doctoral researchers, including 2 as principal supervisor and 2 as co-supervisor, and 11 master's dissertations. Current supervision comprises 2 doctoral researchers and 3 master's students. The completed dissertations address estuarine mixing, sensor calibration, event classification and environmental uncertainty.

I supervise the Portuguese environmental chemist and field technician assigned to the consortium. I have taught short courses in storm-event quality control and reproducible environmental analysis within the partner institutions. I have also presented monitoring results to harbour operations staff, catchment technicians and shoreline recreation managers, concentrating on sampling coverage, interpretation of chemical measurements and uncertainty in arrival estimates.

Record approved by the three institutional signatories on 22 September 2026

## Legal participation

The standing participation agreement was signed on 8 September 2026 by Instituto Marinho de Vale Sereno, Portugal; Universidad de la Ensenada de Lóbriga, Spain; and Brackenquay Institute for Spatial Planning, Ireland. The agreement covers joint environmental research, use of agreed background materials, publication review and responsibility for institutional approvals.

The partners are three independent legal entities in three EU member states. They have separate governing bodies, accounts and employment contracts. None owns or controls either of the others. Their registered offices are in Lisbon, Vigo and Cork respectively. Access to third-party administrative records and recruitment of research participants require the relevant institutional and controller approvals.

## Portuguese coordinating institution

Instituto Marinho de Vale Sereno is an independent nonprofit marine research association established under Portuguese law. Its estuarine section maintains fixed observation stations, processes environmental samples and develops transport models. Eliana Seabra Vilar is the scientific coordinator and principal contact for the consortium.

The institute assigns an oceanographer, an environmental chemist and a field technician to the standing collaboration. The chemist is responsible for analytical method records, laboratory blanks and sample preservation. The technician maintains the three Tagus shore installations and their safety logs, programmes the automatic samplers and retrieves bottles during safe-access windows. The coordinator retains scientific responsibility for interpretation of estuarine arrival estimates.

## Spanish university partner

Universidad de la Ensenada de Lóbriga is an independent university in Vigo. Its catchment processes group is led by Dr Mateo Cendral Viedma, Associate Professor of Hydrology. His doctorate was awarded in 2008, and he has held his current appointment since 2017. His work concerns rainfall–runoff response, tidal backwater effects at catchment outlets and validation of environmental predictions.

The university assigns the hydrology lead, a spatial statistician and station technician Iria Soneira Valcedo. Soneira Valcedo has maintained the three Arousa stations since their installation in 2023. Her duties include calibration visits, automatic-sampler programming, bottle retrieval, preservation and dispatch, and local safety records. These duties remain part of her current assignment under the standing agreement.

Brackenquay Institute for Spatial Planning is an independent nonprofit research institute in Cork. Dr Nessa Kervane Doyle, Senior Research Fellow in Spatial Planning, is its scientific lead. Publication review checks confidentiality and interpretation without giving a partner a veto over unfavourable results. # Final scientific report: Stormwater Transit at Estuary Margins

Project period: 1 January 2023–31 December 2025

Report accepted: 16 February 2026; repository correction incorporated: 4 September 2026

Coordinator: Eliana Seabra Vilar, Instituto Marinho de Vale Sereno

Partner lead: Mateo Cendral Viedma, Universidad de la Ensenada de Lóbriga

## Funding and purpose

The project received EUR 360,000 from the Instituto Marinho de Vale Sereno Research Endowment under internal competitive award IMVS-RE-2023-07. The award included the Spanish university's agreed research contribution through an institutional collaboration contract. The award is closed, with the scientific report accepted and no extension outstanding.

The study examined whether catchment runoff information improved estimates of freshwater-plume arrival at accessible estuarine margins beyond a model using tide and local salinity history alone. It also tested the field procedures needed to attach chemical observations to those arrivals. Its principal endpoint was transport timing, with chemical sampling providing evidence about the composition of water reaching shoreline stations.

## Observational design

Observations during 2024–2025 covered 18 storms at six estuarine stations. Three stations were in the Tagus estuary and three in the Ría de Arousa. Both station groups included an inner margin, an intermediate mixing location and a more seaward margin. These were fixed shore installations. Station positions were selected for safe access and reliable equipment attachment, rather than as a probability sample of either estuary's shoreline.

The 18 storms were Atlantic frontal systems retained only when both study catchment systems met the runoff-separation rule. The Tagus input represented its upstream contributing catchment; the Arousa input combined the Ulla and Umia contributing catchments. Each required a distinct runoff rising limb followed by recession to antecedent flow before the next retained system. Multiple rainfall pulses within that episode belonged to the same storm. Systems producing a qualifying episode in only one study area were outside the paired inventory. Selection was completed without inspecting model errors.

The catchment-event reference time was the rainfall-weighted temporal centroid of the associated rainfall episode, calculated separately for each estuary's contributing catchment system. A shared storm identifier therefore linked two local reference times, rather than imposing simultaneous runoff or arrival on the two estuaries. All timestamps were stored in UTC. This design sampled jointly wet Atlantic systems and did not represent the full range of rare flood extremes or locally confined storms.

Salinity and temperature were logged at 10-minute intervals. A plume arrival was defined as a salinity decrease of at least 2 practical-salinity units below the station's antecedent tidal-phase reference, sustained for at least 30 minutes. The reference was calculated using observations available before the event window. Manual review checked sensor faults and tidal-reference failures without changing thresholds to improve model agreement.

The complete design contained 108 storm–station opportunities. An arrival time could be assigned to 96. Eight opportunities lacked sufficient sensor data because of power or fouling problems, and four did not cross the arrival threshold. These 12 opportunities were excluded from arrival-time error calculations and retained in the inventory with their reasons. Every storm retained at least one identifiable arrival in each estuary. The error estimate is conditional on an identifiable arrival; discrimination between arrivals and non-arrivals remains untested.

## Chemical sampling and quality assurance

There were 216 environmental water samples, comprising two scheduled samples at each storm–station opportunity: 108 samples from the Tagus stations and 108 from Arousa. Automatic samplers collected the scheduled bottles, including at opportunities without a valid arrival timestamp. Sampling windows were established from each catchment's anticipated event period, before the observed arrival was known.

The Portuguese and Spanish station technicians independently programmed and serviced their local equipment. Bottle retrieval followed each station's documented safe-access and preservation limits. Departures from scheduled collection times were recorded in the sample metadata. All environmental storm sampling was shore-based.

The laboratory additionally processed 24 field duplicates and 12 field blanks, giving 252 sample submissions in total. Duplicates and blanks were quality-control material rather than independent environmental observations. Samples were divided into appropriately preserved aliquots for dissolved nutrients and dissolved copper. Nutrients were reported as nitrogen or phosphorus mass concentration, and copper as dissolved metal mass concentration. Salinity supplied the mixing context.

Samples taken at similar salinity could differ in nutrient and copper composition. Timing offsets between scheduled sampling and actual arrival, variable source mixtures and the limited number of samples within each event prevented estimation of event-integrated contaminant loads. The chemistry results support joint interpretation of concentration, sampling time and mixing conditions rather than conversion of salinity into a general contaminant concentration.

## Models and validation

The baseline model used tidal phase and the station's antecedent salinity history. The augmented model added reconstructed catchment discharge, antecedent rainfall and a runoff-to-estuary lag term. Both estimated hours from the relevant estuary's catchment-event reference to observed station arrival. They used the same eligible observations and validation partitions.

Validation used six outer folds, each withholding three complete storms. Withholding a storm removed its records from both estuaries, including all station observations, from fitting and preprocessing estimation. Parameter selection occurred within the training storms. Validation therefore tested transfer between observed storms at the existing stations. Station identity remained available as a model term.

Mean absolute error was first calculated across valid stations within each storm and then averaged across the 18 storms. This gave each storm equal weight despite missing stations. The baseline cross-validated mean absolute error was 4.0 hours, with a bootstrap 95% confidence interval of 3.2 to 5.0 hours. The augmented model's cross-validated mean absolute error was 2.8 hours, with a bootstrap 95% confidence interval of 2.1 to 3.7 hours.

The paired decrease in mean absolute error was 1.2 hours, with a bootstrap 95% confidence interval of 0.5 to 1.9 hours, equivalent at the point estimates to a 30% reduction relative to the baseline. The augmented model had lower storm-level mean absolute error in 14 of 18 storms.

All intervals used the same 2,000 resamples of whole storms and their held-out errors. Each resample retained both models' errors together, preserving the pairing for the difference estimate. Individual station records were not resampled independently. These intervals describe uncertainty in mean performance; they are not predictive intervals for particular arrivals.

## Interpretation and limitations

The models were assessed as retrospective hindcasts using observed rainfall and reconstructed discharge. Their performance does not establish the accuracy or available lead time of an operational forecast driven by rainfall predictions. Events were not issued as live alerts, and no decision threshold was tested with a response agency.

The small number of independent storms limits precision. Results depend on the selected arrival definition and accessible-margin network. Deep-channel transport, vertical plume structure and transfer to an unobserved estuary remain outside the validation. No city drainage sensor stream was included as a predictor.

For shoreline managers, the work establishes the scale of arrival-time uncertainty and the importance of retaining event context alongside a mapped plume. The project evaluated no prospective city intervention and made no causal estimate of adaptation benefits or their distribution across residents.

## Released outputs

The released dataset, *Estuary Margin Storm Records*, version 1.1, contains station observations, sample metadata, chemical results, an event eligibility table and analysis scripts under CC BY 4.0. The correction incorporated on 4 September 2026 repaired descriptive station labels without altering observations or reported errors. Restricted material consists of access-contact details and installation security information. The archived scripts preserve storm partitions and distinguish environmental samples from quality-control submissions.

The accepted final scientific report and the open *Estuary Margin Storm Records* dataset accompany these articles. The report records project-level findings and limitations; the dataset provides environmental observations, sample metadata and reproducibility materials. The publication register links each article to the relevant archive version.

# Resources, access and data governance register

Status recorded 25 September 2026

Custodians: Eliana Seabra Vilar, Mateo Cendral Viedma and Nessa Kervane Doyle

## Field and laboratory resources

The Portuguese and Spanish partners maintain access to the six shore stations used in the completed monitoring programme. Signed access agreements remain valid through 31 December 2030. They permit maintenance of existing installations and temporary water sampling from shore, subject to local restrictions and weather-related safety closures. Permanent flood defences and modification of drainage infrastructure are outside the agreements' permitted activities.

The equipment register lists six multiparameter sondes and six automatic water samplers assigned to these stations. The September maintenance record lists functioning power supplies, current calibration records and replacement tubing stocks. Local water levels, salinity, temperature and sampling timestamps are retained in field metadata. Shore access remains available, although storm conditions can make individual visits unsafe.

The vessel entry records *Margem Serena*, owned by Instituto Marinho de Vale Sereno and used in 2023 to install the Tagus stations. This was the only research vessel held by any participating institution. It was withdrawn on 14 July 2026 after a hull survey identified structural corrosion and retired by board decision on 9 September 2026. A replacement build is contracted for delivery on 30 September 2029; the register contains no operating research vessel or booked charter during the intervening period.

The Portuguese laboratory has facilities for filtered nutrient analysis and dissolved-metal sample preparation, including an inductively coupled plasma mass spectrometer used for the project's copper measurements. Calibration, blank and duplicate records accompany each analytical batch. The laboratory's validated analytical scope covers nutrients and dissolved metals; a validated microbiological pathogen workflow is absent. Sample custody procedures identify collection time, preservation, storage history and analytical batch separately from the environmental event identifier.

## Computing and observational archives

The partners hold the released estuarine observations and complete reproducibility archive. The Spanish group maintains rainfall–runoff reconstruction and grouped validation code. Analyses run on institutional servers. Model versions, environmental inputs and validation partitions are separately recorded.

The open dataset contains environmental station information and excludes personal contact details. Its licence permits reuse with attribution. Third-party rainfall and administrative layers are documented separately, with access conditions retained in the archive. Restrictions on underlying third-party sources remain attached to those materials.

## Drainage and planning materials

The Irish partner retains a controlled research copy of asset and incident records for the 12 Cork subcatchments draining to the Lee estuary. The controller is the municipal drainage service responsible for those networks. Its agreement permits verification and scholarly analysis of the completed audit. Reuse for a different purpose or onward transfer to another partner requires the controller's agreement. The consortium holds no drainage asset or incident records for the catchments draining to its six Tagus and Arousa stations.

Available planning expertise includes drainage-network cleaning, terrain-based flow-path analysis, spatial accessibility measures and facilitated map review. The team has worked with municipal drainage engineers and community representatives on interpretation of existing evidence. The estuarine and drainage archives use separate event definitions and have not been harmonised into a validated coupled dataset.

## Personal data and ethics status

The completed Irish study used aggregated incident summaries for spatial analysis. Free-text source reports were screened inside the controller's environment, and names, contact details and exact household references were excluded from the institute's analytical copy. Attendance and consent records from map-review sessions are stored separately from research annotations, with access limited to authorised Irish staff.

The institute's ethics committee approved the retrospective study on 16 May 2022. Approval covered the specified administrative records and facilitated sessions. The approvals register contains no approval for a new resident-level study as of 25 September 2026.

The institute's personal-data procedure requires a documented purpose and lawful basis, data minimisation, access controls, encryption and a retention schedule approved by the responsible controller. Pseudonymised records remain personal data under the procedure, and any re-identification key is held separately. Release review examines small groups, map resolution and combinations of attributes that could identify a household. Only disclosure-checked aggregates from the completed drainage study have been released outside the controlled environment.

review_issues.where: prior_project.md 'Observational design': 'The Tagus input represented its upstream contributing catchment… Each required a distinct runoff rising limb followed by recession to antecedent flow'; 'Models and validation' (4.0 h and 2.8 h MAE)
review_issues.problem: Taken literally, the Tagus contributing catchment is about 80,000 km², two-thirds of it in Spain. Its flow is heavily regulated by reservoirs in Spain and on the Zêzere. A rainfall-weighted centroid over that basin, and 'recession to antecedent flow' between paired frontal storms, are not hydrologically meaningful. Travel times from such a centroid run to days. A tide-and-salinity baseline with no catchment information would then not achieve a 4.0 h storm-balanced MAE. Because the brief's central question replaces observed inputs with rainfall forecasts, this ambiguity leads proposals to ignore dam regulation.
review_issues.fix: Define the Tagus input as a bounded, mostly unregulated area. For example, use the Sorraia and Trancão catchments plus lateral inflow below a named gauge, with releases from upstream regulation treated as an observed boundary flow. State the typical range of catchment-to-arrival lags in each estuary. Record the regulation as a limitation fact relevant to forecast-driven inputs.

review_issues.problem:
The registry records few of the limitations the stretch rests on, and the task does not say what the stretch gap is. The following are unregistered or not stated anywhere:
- No estuarine observations or water-level records for the Lee; this is only implied by the six stations being in the Tagus and Arousa.
- No coupled flood–drainage or hydrodynamic inundation model or modeller among the eight staff.
- No social-science or qualitative researcher.
- No agreement with any municipal planning or drainage authority in Portugal or Ireland.
- No live alerts issued and no decision threshold tested with a response agency (prior_project.md).
- No city drainage sensor stream used as a predictor (prior_project.md).
- The Irish study's location-dependent under-reporting of incidents (consortium.md, publications.md).
- Only disclosure-checked aggregates released from the drainage study (resources.md).
Without these, a grader cannot check whether a proposal overclaims existing capacity.
review_issues.fix: Add facts, kind existing or gap as appropriate. State explicitly in the dossier: 'the consortium holds no estuarine observations for the Lee' and 'no assigned staff member has coupled flood–drainage modelling or qualitative social-research expertise'. Add a short stretch note in task.yaml naming the gap: flood-drainage modelling, social science, municipal access, drainage records for the Tagus site and estuarine data for the Lee.

review_issues.problem:
Two points weaken the 4.0 h and 2.8 h results that the methodological rationale and T1 rest on.
1. 'The Tagus input represented its upstream contributing catchment.' That is a dam-regulated basin of roughly 80,000 km². A storm-scale rising limb followed by recession to antecedent flow before each of 18 storms in two winters is implausible there. Rainfall-centroid-to-arrival lags would be days and strongly affected by reservoir releases. A baseline using only tidal phase, salinity history and station identity is then unlikely to reach a 4.0 h MAE.
2. The report never gives the scale of the predicted quantity (median or range of hours from reference to arrival per estuary). A reader cannot judge whether a 4.0 h or 2.8 h error is small or large.
review_issues.fix: Define the Tagus input as a specific gauged lower-estuary inflow, e.g. discharge at the estuary head plus named lower tributaries such as the Sorraia or Trancão, with its catchment area. Add per-estuary median and range of observed lags, e.g. 'median 19 h, range 7–41 h', consistent with the reported MAEs.

rejected: The blanket claim that there is no agreement with any municipal planning or drainage authority conflicts with the existing Irish municipal records agreement for the completed retrospective audit. That agreement is retained; the dossier and facts now explicitly record the absence of agreements for joint monitoring, operational data access or adaptation evaluation.
